questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Most of the local festivals in
this culturally rich region are
traditionally celebrated in the January.
No Error
options_hi: Most of the local festivals in
this culturally rich region are
traditionally celebrated in the January.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
Replace “the January” with “January”.

Rule / Concept: Omission of Articles with months, seasons, festivals, subjects, languages, cities, continent, lakes, diseases, meals etc.-

According to the rules of Zero Article (omission), the definite article 'the' is not used before the names of months (January, February, etc.), days of the week, or seasons (Spring, Summer, etc.) when they are used in a general sense. These nouns are considered unique proper names of time periods and do not require a determiner.

Application to the Given Question- Using "the" before the month is grammatically redundant and incorrect in a general statement about when festivals occur.

More Examples for Clarity

We will meet on Monday. (Not: the Monday)

Winter is my favorite season. (Not: The Winter)

Her birthday is in March. (Not: the March)

Things to Remember / Exam Tips-

The "Of" Exception: You only use "the" if the month or season is followed by a qualifying phrase that makes it specific.

Example: "The January of 2024 was particularly cold."

(Here, "the" is correct because we are talking about one specific January).

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: For centuries, the Hindus
are considering the
Ganga a holy river.
No Error
options_hi: For centuries, the Hindus
are considering the
Ganga a holy river.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “are considering” with “consider”

📌 Rule / Concept: Stative Verbs

Stative Nature of "Consider": The verb consider (when it means "to hold an opinion" or "to believe") is a stative verb. Stative verbs describe states that are generally constant, not actions that are happening at a specific moment. Therefore, they are rarely used in the continuous (-ing) form.

💢 Application to the Given Question - By using "are considering," the sentence implies that the Hindus are currently in the process of thinking about whether the Ganga is holy, as if they might change their minds tomorrow. Since this is a deep-seated, permanent religious belief, the continuous tense is logically and grammatically incorrect. It must be in the Simple Present: "consider."

 

REMEMBER THE LIST of Stative verbs:- Think, Believe, Consider, Have, Own, Possess, Look, Seem, Appear, Consist, Contain, Comprise, Feel, Smell, Taste, Sound, Know, Resemble, Like, Love, Want, Agree, Hate, Forgive, Forget, Remember, Depend, Exist etc.

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the given sentence:

"The treasury must have liquidated the distressed assets before the market crashed."
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the given sentence:

"The treasury must have liquidated the distressed assets before the market crashed."
options_en: The distressed assets must have been liquidated before the market crashed.
The distressed assets must be liquidated before the market crashed.
The distressed assets must have liquidated before the market crashed.
The distressed assets had to be liquidated before the market crashed.
options_hi: The distressed assets must have been liquidated before the market crashed.
The distressed assets must be liquidated before the market crashed.
The distressed assets must have liquidated before the market crashed.
The distressed assets had to be liquidated before the market crashed.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

📌 Rule / Concept: Modal Perfect – Active to Passive Conversion
When a sentence contains a modal + have + V³ (e.g., must have liquidated), the passive structure becomes: Object + modal + have + been + V³. The word “been” is compulsory in modal perfect passive constructions. The tense and modality must remain unchanged during conversion.

📌 Application to the Given Question

The treasury must have liquidated the distressed assets before the market crashed. Here, “must have liquidated” is a modal perfect structure. “The distressed assets” is the object and becomes the subject in passive voice. Following the rule, the correct passive form is: modal (must) + have + been + V³ (liquidated). Hence, “must have been liquidated” is the correct transformation. Option (B) removes the perfect aspect. Option (C) omits “been,” making it grammatically incorrect. Option (D) changes the modal and tense structure.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

For modal perfect structures, always use: modal + have + been + V³. Do not drop “been.” Do not change the modal (must → had to). Preserve the original tense and aspect carefully.

questions.q_en: This is precisely the kind of policy shift that unsettles long-term investors, ______?
questions.q_hi: This is precisely the kind of policy shift that unsettles long-term investors, ______?
options_en: isn’t this
isn’t it
doesn’t it
wasn’t it
options_hi: isn’t this
isn’t it
doesn’t it
wasn’t it
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) - “isn’t it”.

📌 Rule / Concept: “This / That” Pronoun Replacement in Question Tags

When the subject of a sentence is this or that, the pronoun used in the question tag is “it”, not “this” or “that”.

In question tags, demonstrative pronouns are replaced with their neutral pronoun form it.

💢 Application to the Given Question -

  • Subject = This

  • Auxiliary used = is

  • Statement is positive → tag must be negative

  • Replace “this” with it in tag

Therefore: isn’t it?

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅- That was an unexpected development, wasn’t it?

Example 2 ✅ - This is your responsibility, isn’t it?

Example 3 ✅ - That was a strategic error, wasn’t it?

🧠 Things to Remember

This / That → always use it in the tag.

  • Repeat the correct auxiliary.

  • Do not repeat the demonstrative pronoun.

questions.q_en: We have not yet been able to explain whether x = y. A larger sample ______ us to make more accurate predictions, and this is why we are beginning sampling again.
questions.q_hi: We have not yet been able to explain whether x = y. A larger sample ______ us to make more accurate predictions, and this is why we are beginning sampling again.
options_en:
had enabled

would enable

would have enabled

will have enabled
options_hi:
had enabled

would enable

would have enabled

will have enabled
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

👉 Replace “_____” with “would enable”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Conditional Sense with Present–Future Reference

This sentence tests conditional meaning based on time reference, not a fixed “if-clause” structure.

When a sentence discusses a current limitation and a future-oriented plan, English uses:

would + base verb to express a hypothetical or potential result that is still achievable.

Key examiner logic:

 

  • would + base verb → possible, unreal but still open
  • would have + past participle → past unreal, opportunity already lost

💢 Application to the Given Question

“A larger sample _____ us to make more accurate predictions, and this is why we are beginning sampling again.”

 

  • “have not yet been able” → the issue is still unresolved
  • “this is why we are beginning sampling again” → action is starting now / future
  • Therefore, the enabling condition is not finished in the past

Using would have enabled would incorrectly suggest:

  • The larger sample existed earlier
  • The chance to improve predictions is already over
    This directly contradicts the reason clause.

Despite receiving repeated warnings from the committee, the contractor continued using substandard materials during the construction of the bridge.
questions.q_hi:

Despite receiving repeated warnings from the committee, the contractor continued using substandard materials during the construction of the bridge.
options_en: Adverb
Conjunction
Preposition
Adjective
options_hi: Adverb
Conjunction
Preposition
Adjective
questions.solution_en:
Answer: C) Preposition

Explanation: A preposition is a word that shows the relationship of a noun or pronoun with another word in the sentence. Prepositions are usually followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund (-ing form).

Here, “despite” is followed by the phrase “receiving repeated warnings.” It shows contrast between the warnings and the contractor’s actions. Therefore, “despite” functions as a preposition.

questions.q_en:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

The technician noticed that one of the _______ in the laboratory _______ malfunctioning at the moment.
questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

The technician noticed that one of the _______ in the laboratory _______ malfunctioning at the moment.
options_en: equipments / is
equipment / are
equipments / are
equipment / is
options_hi: equipments / is
equipment / are
equipments / are
equipment / is
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (D).

The blanks should be filled with "equipment" and "is".

Rule 1: The Uncountable Noun Trap In English, certain nouns are "uncountable" and never take an "s," even when referring to multiple items. Equipment is one of the most common words tested. Even after the phrase "one of the," you cannot say "equipments".

Incorrect: One of the equipments...

Correct: One of the equipment...

Rule 2: "One of" Subject-Verb Agreement The true subject of the sentence is the word "One," not the noun that follows the word "of". Therefore, the verb must be singular to agree with "One".

Logic: One (Singular Subject) + is (Singular Verb).

Why the other options are confusing:

Option (B) [equipment / are]: This uses the correct noun form but incorrectly uses the plural verb "are" to match the mental idea of "many pieces of equipment." However, grammar requires agreement with the word "One".

Correct Sentence: ...one of the equipment in the laboratory is malfunctioning at the moment.

The "No-S" List (Uncountable Nouns)

These nouns are always considered singular and never take an "s," even when they refer to a large quantity.

Category

Nouns that NEVER take "s"

Material/Items

Equipment, Furniture, Luggage, Baggage, Jewellery, Pottery

Abstract/Ideas

Information, Advice, Knowledge, Evidence, Work, Progress

Generalizations

Scenery, Poetry, Machinery, Stationery, Fuel

Food/Materials

Bread, Butter, Food, Paper, Wood, Iron

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"Heavy rains flooded the basement of the regional bank branch."
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"Heavy rains flooded the basement of the regional bank branch."
options_en: The basement of the regional bank branch was flooded by heavy rains.
The basement of the regional bank branch was flooded with heavy rains
The basement of the regional bank branch flooded due to heavy rains.
No passive is possible.
options_hi: The basement of the regional bank branch was flooded by heavy rains.
The basement of the regional bank branch was flooded with heavy rains
The basement of the regional bank branch flooded due to heavy rains.
No passive is possible.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

📌 Rule / Concept: Simple Past – Transitive Verb Passive Formation
In the Simple Past tense, the active structure is: Subject + V² + Object. The passive structure becomes: Object + was/were + V³ (+ by + Subject). Passive is possible only when the verb is transitive (i.e., it takes a direct object). The preposition “by” is used to indicate the agent in standard passive constructions.

📌 Application to the Given Question

Heavy rains flooded the basement of the regional bank branch. Here, “flooded” is used as a transitive verb because it takes “the basement of the regional bank branch” as its direct object. Therefore, passive conversion is possible. The object becomes the subject, and since it is singular, the correct auxiliary is “was.” The correct passive structure is: was + flooded + by heavy rains. Option (B) incorrectly uses “with.” Option (C) changes the sentence into an active intransitive construction. Option (D) is incorrect because “flooded” is transitive in this sentence.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips- Check whether the verb takes a direct object before forming passive. Use was/were + V³ for simple past passive. Use “by” to introduce the agent. Do not confuse transitive and intransitive uses of the same verb.

questions.q_en:
Modern societies often celebrate progress through visible indicators—economic growth, technological penetration, and expanding infrastructure—while quietly overlooking fractures that resist quantification. Social inequality, though frequently acknowledged in rhetoric, is often treated as an abstract concern rather than a lived reality. The persistence of unequal access to education, healthcare, and legal recourse reveals that disparity is not merely a residual flaw of development but, in many cases, its unintended companion. Progress, when unevenly distributed, can deepen the very divides it claims to bridge. Public discourse tends to individualize social failure. Poverty is reframed as lack of effort, marginalization as absence of adaptability, and exclusion as personal deficiency. Such narratives offer moral comfort to the privileged by converting structural disadvantage into personal responsibility. Over time, this framing dulls collective urgency. When inequality is perceived as self-inflicted, social empathy is replaced by conditional sympathy—extended only to those deemed “deserving.” Institutions, meanwhile, respond with procedural solutions that emphasize efficiency over equity. Welfare systems grow increasingly conditional, access mechanisms become more complex, and accountability is measured through compliance rather than outcome. While these approaches appear neutral, they disproportionately burden those already navigating scarcity. The result is a paradoxical system in which assistance exists formally but remains functionally inaccessible to many. The most corrosive consequence of persistent inequality is not material deprivation alone but the erosion of social trust. When large sections of society experience the state as distant or indifferent, civic engagement weakens and resentment quietly accumulates. Addressing social issues, therefore, requires more than policy expansion; it demands a recalibration of how societies assign blame, distribute dignity, and define progress itself.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The judicial committee noted that the evidence presented by
the defense was too much circumstantial to warrant an
immediate acquittal of the accused in the high-profile case.
No Error
options_hi: The judicial committee noted that the evidence presented by
the defense was too much circumstantial to warrant an
immediate acquittal of the accused in the high-profile case.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

👉 Replace “too much” with “much too”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Much too vs. Too much

  • Too much is used as an Adjective before Nouns (specifically uncountable nouns).

  • Much too is used as an Adverb before Adjectives.

simple way to remember this is the "Last Word Rule":

  1. Too much + Noun (e.g., too much work)

  2. Much too + Adjective (e.g., much too heavy)

💢 Application to the Given Question

...the defense was too much circumstantial to warrant...

In this sentence, the word circumstantial is an Adjective (describing the nature of the evidence). According to the rule, we cannot use "too much" to modify an adjective; we must use much too. Therefore, "too much circumstantial" is grammatically incorrect and must be replaced with "much too circumstantial."

Corrected Sentence

The judicial committee noted that the evidence presented by the defense was much too circumstantial to warrant an immediate acquittal of the accused in the high-profile case.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 This task is much too difficult for a beginner to handle alone. (Adjective) ✅

Example 2 There is too much salt in the soup. (Noun) ✅

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1 This room is too much small for all of us. (Small is an adjective) ❌

Wrong example 2 I have much too work to finish by tonight. (Work is a noun) ❌

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • The Adjective Test: If you can put "very" before the word (e.g., very circumstantial, very hot, very tall), it is an adjective, and you must use much too.

  • The Noun Test: If the word represents a thing or quantity (e.g., sugar, noise, patience), use too much

No error
options_hi: The monitor and captain
of our class is
going to meet her.
No error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (D)-The sentence is grammatically correct.

Rule/Concept: Single Article = Single Person

the number of articles determines the number of people. When two titles (like monitor and captain) are joined by "and," but only the first title has an article (The), it means the same person is performing both roles.

Logic Breakdown:

Subject Check: "The monitor and captain" refers to one single individual.

Verb Agreement: Since the subject is singular, the singular verb "is" in segment (C) is perfectly correct.

The "Two-Person" Trap: If the sentence were about two different people, it would have been: "The monitor and the captain are..." Since the second "the" is missing, we must treat it as one person.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The Aryans utilized swift horses in
their military campaigns that was the
primary reason for their tactical superiority.
No Error
options_hi: The Aryans utilized swift horses in
their military campaigns that was the
primary reason for their tactical superiority.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

Replace “that” with “which”.

Rule / Concept: Relative Pronouns Referring to a Clause -

In English grammar, when we want a relative pronoun to refer back to an entire preceding idea or a whole clause (rather than just the noun immediately before it), we must use "which." The relative pronoun "that" cannot be used to refer to a whole sentence or statement; it can only refer to a specific noun or pronoun (the antecedent).

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, what was the primary reason for their superiority? It wasn't just the "campaigns" (plural) themselves. It was the entire fact/action mentioned in the first part of the sentence: "The Aryans utilized swift horses in their military campaigns." Since the relative pronoun is referring to this entire statement as a single reason, "that" is incorrect. It must be replaced with "which."

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: He passed the exam with flying colors, which surprised everyone. (The fact that he passed surprised them).

Example 2 ✅: It rained all day, which ruined our plans for the picnic. (The fact that it rained ruined the plans).

Example 3 ✅: She ignored my advice, which was a very foolish thing to do. (The act of ignoring advice was foolish).

questions.solution_en:

Rule / Concept: Prepositions of Time (At / In / On)

At: Used for precise, specific points in time (clock times, specific moments like noon/midnight, and the end/beginning of a period).

On: Used for specific days and dates (Monday, 15th August, New Year’s Day).

In: Used for non-specific, longer periods of time such as months, years, seasons, centuries, and parts of the day (morning/afternoon/evening).

Application to the Given Question

"...scheduled to commence at 10:00 AM sharp on the first Monday in October..."

Things to Remember / Exam Tips
